questions.title: Afterhyperpolarization follows delayed potassium channel closure
questions.subject: neuro
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Nerve and Muscle Physiology > Action Potential
questions.question: The occurrence of afterhyperpolarization (the undershoot) following an action potential is primarily due to which of the following ionic mechanisms?

options.A: Persistent inward flow of sodium into the cell
options.B: Significantly delayed closure of inward calcium channels
options.C: Delayed closure of the voltage-gated potassium channels that produced repolarization
options.D: Sudden, rapid opening of chloride channels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Persistent sodium influx would keep the membrane depolarized, not drive it below resting potential; sodium channels are inactivated, not persistently open, by this point in the cycle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Delayed calcium channel closure is not the mechanism responsible for the afterhyperpolarization in a typical neuronal action potential; the relevant channels are potassium, not calcium.
explanations.C: Correct. The same voltage-gated potassium channels that drove repolarization close more slowly than they opened, so they remain open briefly after the membrane has already reached resting potential, letting extra K+ leave and driving the membrane transiently past rest, toward the potassium equilibrium potential. This afterhyperpolarization briefly makes the neuron harder to re-excite, contributing to the relative refractory period that follows.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chloride channels are not the primary driver of the afterhyperpolarization; the phenomenon is explained by the lingering open state of the repolarizing potassium channels.

questions.learning_objective: State that the afterhyperpolarization following an action potential is caused by the delayed closure of the same voltage-gated potassium channels that produced repolarization.
